Absorb a hit
Staying stiff through bumps tires the knees and ends sideways. Slow down if you can\'t keep up.
See the bump early.
Just before it, you are already a little flexed.
As the snow rises, bend and let the bump come into the legs.
At the top you can pop — or stay low if you don\'t want air.
In the trough, lengthen the legs to keep contact.
Bumps and lips are taken with the legs, not the back. Absorbing means staying on the snow when you want to.
Think quiet. Less noise on the bumps means better absorption.
Hands stay in front of you. If they go back, the pop goes with them.
Backflip

Common mistakes: looking at the sky and never spotting, flipping late, reaching with the hands, under-rotating onto the neck, trying it tired or to impress someone. Bail-out: if you are not around, do not stick the arms. Chin in. Try to take it on the back and hips and slide, then get off the landing. If you are unsure before you leave the lip, do not pop.
On the trampoline, a coach sets the hips and teaches a layout or the tuck they want. You do not invent it from a video.
Learn to spot: as you leave, the eyes find the landing over the shoulder early. If you only see sky, you are late.
The set is up and slightly back, from the pop, not a desperate throw of the head on the lip.
Bail on the trampoline until it is boring: if the rotation is late, the spotter stops you, or you sit the rotation down. You practice the bail, not only the make.
Water ramp or airbag next, same coach, same cues. Count consistent landings there before anyone says the word snow.
On snow: helmet and back protector, a jump you straight-air without thinking, steep landing, coach on the side, one rider, speed from a marked start. If any of that is missing, you straight-air it.
A backward flip. Expert, and only with supervision. Trampoline with a spotter, then water or an airbag, then snow with a coach. Never the first try on a resort kicker.
A coach who has never seen you straight-air that jump does not get to say go.
Stop for the day after one scary attempt. The second one, rattled, is how people get hurt.
Age and a club\'s rules come before this page. If they say not yet, it is not yet.
50-50 on a box
First session: helmet, and someone watching. If you are sideways, you exit. You don\'t force a finish.
Pick a low, straight box with a flat start.
Look at the exit, not your skis.
Get on in the middle, skis parallel, equal weight on both feet.
Soft knees, low arms. You don\'t jump onto the box: you roll onto it.
At the end, let the box go and absorb the small drop.
The 50-50: both skis in line, in the middle of the box, like a very wide flat rail.
A bit of speed, not a crawl. Too slow and the skis stick or wander.
Eyes dropping to the tips tip you forward.
Cork 360
A cork is not a style you add because a clip looked good. Off-axis plus too little rotation is a shoulder or a neck. Doubles, cork 720s and rodeos are not in this app.
Prerequisite: 360s you land without fighting, both directions, plus a stable grab. If the 360 is still a throw, you do not add cork.
The axis is learned on a trampoline or an airbag with a coach, not by \'leaning back\' on an XL in the park.
You pop up first, like a 360. The tilt is small and set by the coach. More axis is not the goal of the first reps.
Spot the landing. Under-rotation is the common injury: you come down on a shoulder or the upper back, sideways.
Bail: if you are not around, don\'t post an arm. Chin in, try to slide on the back, get off the line. If you felt late on the lip, you should have ridden straight.
Snow only on a small jump you 360 cleanly, with the same coach who saw the airbag reps, and with the landing steep and empty.
An off-axis 360: the body tilts so the head passes below the feet for a moment. It is not a full flip, and it is still an inversion. Basics of the axis only, with a coach, after clean 360s.
If the straight 360 is your proudest trick, keep it. The cork can wait a season.
Helmet and back protector are on before the first off-axis attempt, including on an airbag.
Fall without snapping
Planting a hand to \'catch yourself\' breaks a wrist or a thumb. You accept the slide.
Tuck the arms. Thumbs along the hands, not stuck out.
Fall to the side, hip and thigh, and let yourself slide.
Chin toward the chest so the back of the helmet hits before the neck.
Don\'t stand up while you are still on a jump or rail line.
You will fall. The goal is to slide, not to post a hand.
Practice falling on a gentle slope, slow, before the park.
If you are unsure about pain in the head, neck or back: stop and call. Not \'one more run\'.

Not on day one of a feature, not without a helmet, not if the 360 still fails half the time. If nobody experienced can watch, stay on the 360. Inverted tricks are later in this library: trampoline, airbag, then snow with a coach. Not alone.
Prerequisite: a clean 360 left and right, and a solid switch landing.
Same pop as a 360. The spin comes from the head and hips, not a late throw.
You pass the 360 and keep going until you see the landing in switch.
Block the shoulders, skis together, land switch in the middle.
Get off the line before you celebrate.
One and a half turns. You land switch. Only when 360s are calm both ways, on a small jump, with someone watching.
Under-rotating a 540 means landing sideways in switch. A committed 360 is better.
Speed is your straight-air speed on THIS jump. Not an extra push \'for the spin\'.
Frontflip

Do not learn this by \'throwing your head\' on a park jump. That is how people land on their face or their neck. A parent or coach decides if you are in a program that teaches it. This page is the order, not a permission.
On the trampoline the coach teaches the set: pop up, a small tuck, eyes finding the landing in front of you, not a dive at the mat.
Over-rotation onto the face is the usual mistake. The head does not lead. The pop does.
Practice the bail with the spotter: if you are late, you do not reach. You take it on a shoulder and roll, chin tucked.
Only move to water or an airbag when the trampoline flip is consistent and the bail is a choice, not a surprise.
Snow is a jump you already straight-air, steep landing, coach watching, helmet on. The approach speed is the straight-air speed.
If the set does not feel there on the lip, you ride it straight. A half-committed frontflip is a face-first landing.
A forward flip. The face is what you risk. Same ladder as the backflip: trampoline with a coach, then water or airbag, then snow only with that coach. Harder to spot than a backflip.
If you cannot spot the landing on the trampoline, you are not ready for airbag, and you are nowhere near snow.
One clean attempt does not mean five more. Fatigue makes the head dive.
Stop if you are trying it to match a friend. Their airbag reps are not yours.
Inversions: the order
No app replaces a person who can say \'not today\'. Listen to them. Emergency numbers stay in the phone: 144 and 1414 in Switzerland, 112 in France.
First the trampoline, with a coach or a trained spotter who can catch you. You learn to set, to spot the landing, and to bail.
Then a water ramp or an airbag, still with that coach. Snow is not the place to discover the rotation.
Snow comes last: a jump you already straight-air cleanly, a steep landing, a coach who says go, speed checked, nobody below.
If you hesitate on the approach, you ride out. The decision is made before you drop, not on the lip.
Many coaches will not teach this until the basics are boring and you are old enough for their program. That is the program, not an insult.
Backflips, frontflips and corks are in this app. They are advanced, and they are done with a coach. The order does not change because a video looks easy.
Film the basics (straight air, 180, 360). Progress shows there before any magazine trick.
Fear is information. If you don\'t want to go, you don\'t owe anyone a jump.
Japan
If the japan puts you on the back edge, stop. Go back to the mute until your axis is neutral.
Straight air, high calm pop. No spin.
The front hand finds the end of the front ski, on the outside.
The front knee opens slightly. The back ski stays close.
Don\'t pull the ski behind you until you lose the horizon.
Let go, parallel, land in the middle of the ski.
The japan: you grab the front tip, outside, and the knee opens a little. Pretty, and only after a stable mute.
It is a style grab, not a grab to \'go bigger\'. The landing matters more than the photo.
Keep the other hand low so you don\'t start a 180 by accident.
Landing
Landing stiff means the knee takes the hit instead of the spring. If you are too long, take a slightly low landing rather than reaching for the flat.
In the air, prepare the legs: not locked, not glued to your hips.
Find the slope with the skis. They land along the landing, not flat on the flat.
On contact, flex ankle, knee, hip, in that order, like a spring.
Hands stay low and in front. They do not go to the sky.
Once you are stable, get off the line.
A good landing is soft in the legs and steady in the eyes. The ski touches, the body follows.
The sound should be dull, not a slap. A slap means stiff legs.
After three bad landings in a row, change feature or stop.
Mute grab
A grab that makes you miss the landing is not a grab. Shorten it.
Start from a stable straight air, safety already clean.
Bring the front ski to the front hand. The knee comes to the chest.
Grab the outside of the ski, not between the legs.
The other arm opens a little for balance, without starting a spin.
Let go early, skis parallel, absorb.
The mute: the front hand grabs the front ski, outside edge, between tip and binding.
Knee up, not a broken back reaching for the ski.
The mute should not open the hip enough to cross the skis.
Nollie
Too much weight forward and you plant the tips. Keep the hands in front of the hips, not over your head.
In a straight line, move the hips a little forward to load the front of the skis, without going over.
Pop by extending the ankles. The tails rise first.
Bring the knees up, skis flat.
Land in the middle of the ski.
Alternate ollie and nollie on the flat until they are the same height.
A nollie pops from the tips. It is the ollie reversed, and it prepares switch.
A nollie is easier to feel if you are already low before the pop.
If it leaves crooked, your shoulders turned. Keep them parallel to the skis.
Nose butter
Butters happen away from other people. A sweeping tail hits someone\'s shins.
Find a small bump or a soft side of the piste, almost flat at the exit.
Move weight onto both tips, knees bent, back fairly upright.
Let the tails break loose and turn. Guide with the feet and the eyes.
Keep enough speed that you don\'t stop in the middle.
Bring the tails back in line before the bump ends, and return the weight to the middle.
A nose butter slides on the tips and pivots the tails. Slow, on a soft bump.
If you go over the front, you were too far forward and too stiff. Stay low.
Aim for a small angle first, not a 360 butter.
Ollie
Learn the ollie on the flat, away from people, before you take it to a lip.
In a straight line, medium speed, flex a little.
Push the feet forward to load the tails, without sitting down.
Extend ankles and knees at once. The tip rises, the tail follows.
Bring the knees up so the skis stay with your feet.
Land flat, both skis together, and absorb.
An ollie is a pop from the tails. It helps on a small hit, a bump, or leaving a box.
If only the tip leaves the snow, you pulled with your back. The pop comes from the legs.
A small clean ollie beats a big off-balance hop.
The 180 is first on an S jump, both directions, before a bigger feature.
You already ski a bit of switch, at least on a mellow blue, so the landing isn\'t a surprise.
On a small jump, pop straight, then turn the head and shoulders. The skis follow.
Hips turn with the shoulders. Not only the arms.
Aim for 180, not 270. Lock the eyes on the landing.
Land switch, weight in the middle, and ride straight for a few metres.
A half turn in the air. You leave forward and land switch — the other way comes later.
Pick an easy direction (often looking over the front shoulder) and clean it before the other way.
If you under-rotate, the head left late, not the feet.
Park rules
In Switzerland: 144 for an ambulance, 1414 for REGA helicopter. In nearby France: 112. Save the numbers before you go up.
Check the day\'s map at the bottom. Features are sized S, M, L, XL. Start on S.
Look uphill and downhill before you drop. One look, then you go.
Don\'t cross a jump or a rail. Ride the line, exit, and clear to the side.
If you fall, get off the line immediately, even if it hurts. The rider behind cannot see you in time.
One rider at a time on a feature. Wait until the landing is empty.
A terrain park is not a normal piste. Everyone goes the same way, and nobody stops on a landing.
Helmet buckled before the first chair, not \'only for the park\'.
If the snow is hard or you are tired, the park can wait. Most bad falls are at the end of the day.
Helmet and back protector
A beanie under the helmet is not a helmet. Landing bumps are often hard in the afternoon.
The helmet does not shift when you shake your head. The strap is closed.
The back protector covers the middle of the back, not only the shoulders.
Knee and hip padding helps the day you learn butters and switch.
Buckle the boots tight. Play in the shell and the landing goes sideways.
A fitted ski helmet, a back protector, and full gloves. Not optional if you jump or slide.
If the helmet took a hard hit, replace it. The foam can be dead without looking broken.
Gloves with a reinforced palm save an open hand on a rail.
50-50 on a rail
Don\'t learn on a tall round rail. A slip there cuts. Stay on a low tube or a narrow box.
A low rail, not too long, with an entry you can roll.
Steady speed. Aim the middle of both skis at the middle of the rail.
Look at the exit. Feet flat, soft knees.
If you start to slip off, don\'t fight it: jump off to the side.
The exit absorbs like a small landing.
Same idea as the box, but the rail is narrow. Only after a straight box feels easy.
The sound should be continuous. A knock means a ski biting the edge.
Ask someone if you are getting on crooked. You should not look at your skis.
Read a jump
Never stop on the flat just after a lip, or on the landing. The next rider is faster than you think.
Stop on the side, never on the track, and look at the lip then the landing.
See where the slope continues. If you cannot see the bottom, you do not go.
Watch two riders to learn the speed: too short, or too long.
Pick a start point. Too high means too fast. Too low and you land on the flat.
The first hit is straight, no grab and no spin.
The jump is won before the lip. You pick the speed, you see the landing, you decide.
A clean S jump beats a missed M.
Headwind or flat light hides the landing. Wait.
Safety grab
If you lose the slope while grabbing, the grab was too early or too low. Let go and land.
Start on a small straight air you already land without thinking.
In the air, bend the knees and bring the ski to the hand. Don\'t dive the hand down and break the back.
Front or back hand grabs the inside of the ski, in front of the binding.
Hold it for a second, let go, set up the landing.
Eyes stay on the landing the whole time.
The safety is grabbing the ski just in front of the binding, between the feet. The most stable grab to start with.
Knees up, torso quiet. The grab should not turn your shoulders.
Do the safety on both sides before you change grabs.
Box slide
A slide on a thin rail comes after weeks of boxes. A ski edge catches, and the fall is hard.
A clean 50-50 on this same box, both feet forward.
Get on in 50-50, then turn shoulders and hips together to about 90°.
Weight stays in the middle of the skis. Don\'t sit downhill.
Look at the exit over the front shoulder.
Bring the skis back in line before the end. A switch exit is later.
The slide: skis across the box, like a skid set down on it. Almost flat at first, rotation very slow.
Skid on the snow beside the box to feel 90° before you get on.
Too much rotation at the start puts you at 180 before the middle. Turn less, earlier.
Straight air
No violent pop on a jump you don\'t know. Roll it almost flat first, then add a little air.
Arrive athletic: ankles, knees and hips a little bent, hands in front.
Look at the end of the landing, not your tips.
On the lip, push down (the pop) and let the skis come with you. Don\'t throw the shoulders back.
In the air, soft knees, skis parallel, weight in the middle.
Both skis touch first, then you flex to absorb.
Straight air is the base of everything else: pop, quiet body, eyes far away.
If you leave backwards, your eyes and hips stayed on the lip. Look far ahead.
Film yourself from the side. You\'ll see a broken waist immediately.
Switch 180
The switch approach is the real risk: you see other people less well. Look twice before you go.
Clean switch on a blue, and ollie or nollie already there.
Small jump. Arrive switch, pop, the head turns toward your usual direction.
The skis pass 180 and find forward again.
Land like a normal straight air and absorb.
Both directions before a bigger jump.
You leave switch and land forward. Often easier than a regular 180, because the landing is your strong direction.
If the approach is wrong, you don\'t \'send it anyway\'. You roll the jump with no pop.
Keep the spin small and high. A flat switch 180 ends with a planted tail.
Skiing switch
Switch tires muscles you don\'t usually use. Stop before you cut someone off.
On the flat, slide switch just to feel which foot is forward.
Ski a whole green run switch, wide turns.
Hands low, a bit more weight on the uphill ski, like forwards — mirrored.
Do traverses, then small carved turns.
When a green switch is boring, move to an easy blue. Not before.
Switch means the other foot in front. Without it, 180s and slides stay guesses.
Five minutes each lift beats one hour on the last day of the trip.
Look far. In switch the eyes drop toward the back tip.
Tail butter
Sitting on the tails locks the ski and dumps you backward. Stay standing in the boots.
On a soft bump, move weight to the tails without sitting down.
Bend the knees and let the tips get light.
Turn the tips with the feet. The upper body stays fairly quiet.
Look where you want to come out.
Put the tips back down before the bump ends and recenter.
A tail butter loads the tails. The tips lift and turn. Same idea as the nose, reversed.
Low arms stop you from arching.
A tiny tail butter held for a long time beats a big missed gesture.
No 360 on an M until the 360 on an S is calm, one direction, ten times in a row.
Small jump, straight-air speed, pop up before you spin.
Head first, then shoulders, then hips. The skis follow.
Pick a spot on the landing and find it again at the end of the turn.
Keep the skis together. A trailing ski kills the spin, or finishes it too early.
Block the upper body when you see the slope again, and land in the middle.
A full turn. You land the way you left. It needs a clean 180 both ways.
Under-rotating is normal at first. Add the head, not a violent shoulder throw.
If you over-rotate, you popped late and spun early. Pop first.
Open Shortcuts
For a Cardo or Bluetooth headset. Music stays on.
Siri
Say the phrase and the app name. The button opens Shortcuts.
Voice
